name: C
year_note: Developed 1969–1973 at Bell Labs alongside Unix; first widely described in K&R (1978).
tagline: A portable, close-to-the-metal systems language that became the lingua franca of computing.
summary: C is a small, statically typed, imperative language designed to write the Unix operating system. It exposes memory through pointers while abstracting over machine instructions, which made both Unix and C itself portable across hardware. Its syntax — braces, semicolons, for loops, ++ — became the template for most mainstream languages that followed.
history:
Dennis Ritchie created C at Bell Labs between 1969 and 1973 as an evolution of Ken Thompson's B, adding a type system (char, int, structs, pointers) that B's word-oriented design lacked on the byte-addressed PDP-11. In 1973 the Unix kernel was rewritten in C, one of the first operating system kernels written in a high-level language.

The 1978 book 'The C Programming Language' by Brian Kernighan and Ritchie served as the de facto standard ('K&R C') until ANSI standardized the language in 1989 (C89/C90). Later ISO revisions added // comments, inline and variable-length arrays (C99), threads and atomics (C11), and bool/nullptr/constexpr-style features (C23).
innovations: Made a high-level language the standard way to write operating systems (Unix kernel, 1973)
A typed pointer model with pointer arithmetic, bridging assembly and high-level code
The brace-and-semicolon syntax adopted by C++, Java, C#, JavaScript, Go and many others
The C preprocessor and header-file model of separate compilation
The C ABI, still the common interface for calling between languages

typing.notes: Implicit conversions and unchecked casts make it weakly typed; C23 added `auto` for simple inference.

influenced_by.note: C began as 'NB' (new B), adding types to B.
B's parent; source of much of the terse syntax.
Ritchie credited ALGOL 68 for the type composition model (structs/unions).

influenced_by_external.name: Assembly (PDP-11)
influenced_by_external.note: Operators like ++ map naturally onto PDP-11 addressing modes (though they predate it in B).

influenced_by_external.name: PL/I
influenced_by_external.note: Via Multics; the -> operator and some syntax.

generics.note: Only `_Generic` type-dispatch selection and void* / macros; no parametric types.

first-class-functions.note: Function pointers can be passed and stored, but there are no closures or lambdas.

modules.note: Only via separate compilation units, header files and `static` linkage.

coroutines.note: setjmp/longjmp or ucontext; not part of the language.

milestones.event: Development of B-successor begins at Bell Labs
C23 published: bool/true/false keywords, nullptr, constexpr, typeof

trivia: The name follows B; Ritchie considered whether its successor should be 'D' or 'P' (following BCPL).
Kernighan and Ritchie's book popularized 'hello, world' as the first example program.
